label: def:semimeasure
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:semimeasure}
  A  {\em semimeasure} is a function $P:\{0,1\}^* \rightarrow \mathbb R_{\ge 0}$ that satisfies 
  $P(\text{empty str}) \le 1$ and $P(x) \ge P(x0) + P(x1)$, 
  where $xb$ denotes the concatenation of string $x$ and bit $b$.
head: environment

title: Question
body_md:
Does conditional probability $1 - M(\omega_{\scaleobj{0.8}{\le}n})/M(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n})$ decrease rapidly to zero on the bits that are fixed by some computable pattern? 
  For example, if each even bit equals the preceding odd bit, does the sum remain bounded?
head: environment

label: th:main_exponential
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:main_exponential}
  Fix $\gamma > 1$. 
  Let $T \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ be decided by a program of length~$k$. 
  If all prefixes of $\omega \in \{0,1\}^\infty$ are in $T$, then
  \[
    \sum_{n:\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T} \left(M(\bar \omega_n \,|\, \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n})\right)^{\gamma} \le O(k^{2\gamma} 2^{\gamma k}) 
  \]
  and 
  \[
    \sum_{\substack{n:\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T\\n \le N}} M(\bar \omega_n \,|\, \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}) \le O(k^22^k \log^2 N \log^2 \log N).
  \]
head: environment

label: th:main_L1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:main_L1}
  There exists a computable leafless tree $T \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ and infinitely many strings $w$ in $T$ such that
  \[
    \sum_{\substack{n:w_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}\bar w_n \not\in T\\n \le |w|}} M(\bar w_n \,|\, w_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}) \ge \Omega\left(\tfrac {\log |w|} {\log^2 \log |w|}\right).
  \]
head: environment

label: th:classifiers_upper
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:classifiers_upper}
  Fix $\gamma>1$ and a computable time bound~$t$. 
  If $f: \{0,1\}^* \rightarrow \{0,1\}$ is computed by a $k$-bit program in time $t(k,|z|)$ on input~$z$, then for $x_1, x_2, \ldots \in \{0,1\}^*$, 
  \[
    \sum_{n=1}^\infty \big(1 - M(f(x_n) \,|\, h_{n}, x_n)\big)^{\gamma} \le O(k^{1+\gamma} \log^{2\gamma} k), 
  \]
  where $h_n = [x_1, f(x_1), \ldots, x_{n-1}, f(x_{n-1})]$.
head: environment

label: cor:classifiers_lower
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:classifiers_lower}
  There exists a computable classifier $f$ and infinitely many $N$ for which there exist strings $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N \in \{0,1\}^*$ such that 
  \[
    \sum_{n=1}^N M(1-f(x_n) \,|\, h_n, x_n) \ge \Omega \left(\frac {\log N} {\log^2 \log N}\right),
  \]
  where $h_n = [x_1, f(x_1), \ldots, x_{n-1}, f(x_{n-1})]$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the game with $s = \gamma = 1$ and the single tree $T = \{\text{empty str.}, 0, 00, 000, \ldots\}$.
Bob wins by concentrating all measure along the tree, thus setting $B(x) = 1$ for all $x \in T$.
head: manual

title: Example
body_md:
Again, let $s = \gamma = 1$. Consider the game with an arbitrary single tree. 
If Alice evaluates a computable rational measure~$A$, then Bob has a computable winning strategy
by splitting his flow proportionally to $A$'s flow in nodes $x$ for which both children are in the tree, 
and otherwise, if $x$ has only 1 child, sending all flow in this child's direction.
head: manual

label: lem:game2thm_1tree
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:game2thm_1tree}
  Fix $\gamma \ge 1$ and a constant~$s$. 
  Assume that for each tree $T$, Bob has a winning strategy in the game with 1 tree~$T$ and value~$s$, 
  and that these strategies are uniformly computable given~$T$. 
  Then for each computable $T$ and infinite branch~$\omega$ in~$T$, 
  \[
    \sum_{n:\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T} \big(M(\bar \omega_n \,|\, \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n})\big)^{\gamma} \le O\big(2^{\gamma\operatorname{K}(T)}s\big). 
  \]
head: environment

label: lem:MdomP
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:MdomP}
  For all lower semicomputable semimeasures $B$ and $x$,
  \[
    2^{-\operatorname{K}(B)}B(x) \le O(M(x)). 
  \]
  where $\operatorname{K}(B)$ is the minimal prefix complexity of a program that lower approximates~$B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the game for a computable tree $T$. 
  Let Alice play a strategy in which she ignores $T$ and Bob's moves:
  she computes a lower approximation of~$M$ and in each round, sets the current values equal to~$A$. 

  Bob plays the winning strategy. 
  We obtain a semimeasure~$B$ by taking the limit of his semimeasure. 
  It satisfies
  \[
    \sum_{n:\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T} \left(\frac {M(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n)} {B(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}0) + B(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}1))} \right)^{\gamma} \le s. 
  \]
  Note that $\operatorname{K}(B) \le \operatorname{K}(T) + O(1)$, because $B$ is computed from $T$ by evaluating the strategy.
  Hence,  lemma~\ref{lem:MdomP} implies
  \[
    M(\bar \omega_n \,|\, \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}) \le 2^{\operatorname{K}(T)}
    \frac {M(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar \omega_n)} { B(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} 0) + B(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} 1)}
                                                                            
  \]
  The lemma finishes by raising to the power $\gamma$ and summing.
head: environment

label: lem:game2thm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:game2thm}
  Fix $\gamma \ge 1$, a computable function $s : \mathbb N \rightarrow \mathbb Q$, and a uniformly computable sequence of trees $T_1, T_2, \ldots$
  Suppose Bob wins each game with parameters $\gamma, s_\ell$ and trees $T_1, \ldots, T_{2^{2^\ell}}$. 
  Also suppose that the strategies are uniformly computable in~$\ell$. 
  Then, for each tree $T_j$ and each infinite branch $\omega$ in $T_j$, 
  \[
    \sum_{n:\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T_j} (M(\bar \omega_n \,|\, \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}))^{\gamma} \le O(\ell^{2\gamma} s_\ell). 
  \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is similar as for lemma~\ref{lem:game2thm_1tree}, but with a different estimate for the complexity of Bob's semimeasure. 
  Now the trees and the strategies are uniformly computable in $\ell$, thus this complexity is bounded by the complexity of~$\ell$. 
  Hence, $\operatorname{K}(B_\ell) \le \operatorname{K}(\ell) + O(1) \le 2\log \ell + O(1)$. 
  After taking exponents and $\gamma$ powers, this corresponds to the factor~$O(\ell^{2\gamma})$ in the right side.
head: environment
name: Proof sketch.

label: lem:game_lowerbound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:game_lowerbound}
  Let tree $T$ and function $s$ be computable. 
  Assume that for all $N$,
  Alice has a strategy in which for all $N$ there exits an $N$-bit string $z$ in $T$ such that for infinitely many rounds,
  \begin{equation}\tag{$*$}\label{eq:winning}
    \sum_{\substack{z_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}\bar z_n \not\in T\\n \le N}} \left(\frac {A(z_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar z_n)} {B(z_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}0) + B(z_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}1)}\right)^{\gamma} \;>\;s_N, 
  \end{equation}
  If these strategies are uniformly computable given $N$, 
  then for all $N$, there exists an $N$-bit $z$ in $T$ such that
  \[
    \sum_{n:z_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}\bar z_n \not\in T} (M(\bar z_n \,|\, z_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n}))^{\gamma} \ge \Omega(s_N2^{-\gamma \operatorname{K}(N)}).
  \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider a game in which Bob plays blindly, and lower approximates a priori probability~$M$. 
  Alice plays the winning strategy. 
  Since Alice's semimeasure $A$ is lower semicomputable given~$N$, lemma~\ref{lem:MdomP} implies
  \[
    M(x) \ge \Omega (2^{-\operatorname{K}(N)}A(x)), 
  \]
  The proof finishes by substituting this, raising to the power $\gamma$ and summing.
head: environment

label: lem:weightflow2flowflow_Bob
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is a simple formal verification. 
  Let $A_{\textnormal{ff}}$ be Alice's strategy in a flow-flow game with a single tree~$T$. 
  We need a winning strategy $B_{\textnormal{ff}}$ for Bob in this game. 

  First $A_{\textnormal{ff}}$ is transformed to a strategy $w$ for Alice in the weight-flow game. 
  Recall that $b$ is always a bit. 
  For each node $xb$ in $\partial T$ with $x\bar b \in T$, Alice sets $w(x) = A_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb)$. She keeps $w(x)=0$ for all other~$x$.
 
  Bob plays his winning strategy $B_{\textnormal{wf}}$ against~$w$. 
  He obtains a strategy $B_{\textnormal{ff}}$ by ``pushing $B_{\textnormal{wf}}$ one step forward'' 
  when the relevant direction in $T$ is unique. More precisely, $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(\epsilon) = B_{\textnormal{wf}}(\epsilon)$
  \\-- $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb) = 0$ if $xb \not\in T$, 
  \\-- $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb) = B_{\textnormal{wf}}(xb)$ for nodes $xb \in T$ with a brother, thus if $x \bar b \in T$, 
  \\-- $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb) = B_{\textnormal{wf}}(x)$ for nodes $xb \in T$ without brother. 

  Note that $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(y) \ge B_{\textnormal{wf}}(y)$ for $y \in T$ and that $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(y) > B_{\textnormal{wf}}(y)$ only happens if $y$ is in $T$ and has no brother in $T$. 
  This implies $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x) \ge B_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb) + B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x \bar b)$ for all $x$, because if $x\bar b \not\in T$, then $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(p \bar b) = 0$. 

  In the sum that defines the winning condition, only values $B_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb)$ are used for which $xb$ has no brother. Thus we have
  \[
    \frac {A_{\textnormal{ff}}(x\bar b)} {B_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb) + B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x\bar b)} \le  \frac {w(x)} {B_{\textnormal{wf}}(x)}.  
  \]
  Since these are precisely the terms we care about in the winning condition, Bob wins in the flow-flow game.
head: environment

label: lem:weightflow2flowflow_Alice
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be the tree with zeros in even positions, thus $T = \{z : 0 = z_2 = z_4 = \ldots = z_{2\lfloor |z|/2 \rfloor}\}$.\footnote{
    Any tree could be used in which each infinite branch infinitely often alternates between having 1 and 2 children.
    For example, the tree with repeated positions. 
    The above tree was chosen for notational convenience. 
  }
  The idea is to associate strings $x$ in the weight-flow game to expanded strings
  \[
    x_{\text{exp}} = 00x_10x_20 \cdots 0x_{|x|}
  \]
  in the flow-flow game. Alice's weights $w$ in $x$ become flows in $w(x_{\text{exp}} 1)$, since $x_{\text{exp}} 1 \in \partial T$.  
  We explain in detail that this works. 

  Consider a strategy $B_{\textnormal{ff}}$ for Bob in the flow-flow game with the tree from the lemma. 
  Let Bob play the strategy
  \[
    B_{\textnormal{wf}}(x) = B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}0) + B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}1). 
  \]
  against Alice's winning strategy $w$ in the weight-flow game. 

  Note that the set of $\{x_{\text{exp}}1: x \in \{0,1\}^*\}$ is prefix-free. 
  Alice's strategy in the flow-flow game is obtained by setting
  \begin{align*}
    A_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}1)  &= w(x) \text{ for all $x \in \{0,1\}^*$}, \\
    A_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}1z) & = 0 \text{ for all $x \in \{0,1\}^*$ and z-nonempty},
  \end{align*}
  and all other values of $A_{\textnormal{ff}}$ are obtained by recursively summing over the values of the children. 
  This implies that $A_{\textnormal{ff}}(\text{empty string}) \le 1$ by the requirement of~$w$. 

  In the winning condition in the flow-flow game, we only sum over prefixes $x$ of odd length, 
  since precisely the nodes $x$ with odd $|x|$ have 1 child. Moreover, this child is always $x0$, 
  thus the winning condition in the flow-flow game only consists of terms of the form
  \[
    \frac {A_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}1)} {B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}0) + B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x_{\text{exp}}1)} = \frac {w(x)} {B_{\textnormal{wf}}(x)}.  
  \]
  Since Alice plays a winning strategy $w$, the sum of $\gamma$-powers of the right-hand side exceeds $s$ and the $A_{\textnormal{ff}}$ strategy is also winning $B_{\textnormal{ff}}$. 
  Because we started with an arbitrary strategy~$B_{\textnormal{ff}}$, the lemma is proven.
head: environment

label: lem:upper_bound_eps
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:upper_bound_eps}
  For each $\varepsilon > 0$, Bob has a winning strategy in the weight-flow game for $\gamma = 1+\varepsilon$ and $s = 2^{\gamma} (\tfrac {8} {(1-2^{-\varepsilon})^3} + 3)$.
head: environment

label: lem:weightflow_easy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weightflow_easy}
 For each integer $C \ge 1$, Bob has a winning strategy in this variant of the weight-flow game.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
With  {\em pushing flow $\delta$ to node $x$}, we mean increasing $B(z) \leftarrow B(z) + \delta$ for all prefixes~$z \sqsubseteq x$. 
  The idea of Bob's reply is to push minimal flows to prevent Alice's winning condition from happening.  
  Thus each time he finds $x_1, \ldots, x_C$ that satisfies this condition, 
  and pushes the minimal flow to $x_C$ so that $w(x_j)/B(x_j) = 1/C$ for some~$j$. 
  In case there are several such $C$-tuples, it does not matter which one is selected first. 
  \begin{algorithm}[H]
    \caption{Bob's reply in the variant of the game.} 
    \begin{algorithmic}[1]
	  \While{strings $x_1 \sqsubset \cdots \sqsubset x_C$ exist with $w(x_j) >B(x_j)/C$ for all $j = 1, \ldots, C$} 
	     \State $\delta\;\;\;\;\;\; \gets \min \{Cw(x_j) - B(x_j): j = 1, \ldots, C\}$
	     \State $B(z) \gets B(z) + \delta$ for all $z \sqsubseteq x_C$ 
	  \EndWhile
    \end{algorithmic}
  \end{algorithm}

  By construction, Alice's winning requirement is never satisfied. 
  We verify that $B$ is always a semimeasure.
  Note that $B(z) \ge B(z0) + B(z1)$ holds for all $z$, because each time a flow $\delta$ is pushed through $z0$ or $z1$, 
  also $B(z)$ is increased. 

  Let $\epsilon$ denote the empty string. 
  It remains to prove that $B(\epsilon) \le 1$. 
  Let $\delta_t$ be the value of $\delta$ in line 2 during the $t$-th push of flow in $B$, (in all replies combined). 
  Now it is explained that
  \[
    \sum_x w(x) \ge \sum_x \max \Big(0,  w(x) - \frac {B(x)}{C} \Big) + \sum_{t} \delta_t. 
  \]
  Initially both sides are zero. 
  At each increase of $w(x)$, the left side can only increase more. 
  Each time some flow $\delta_t$ is pushed, the right side can only decrease, 
  because there are $C$ different strings~$x_j$ where $B(x_j)$ 
  increases by~$\delta_t$ and where~$Cw(x_j) \ge B(x_j) + \delta_t$. 
  Hence, the above inequality always holds. 

  By definition of the game, the left side is at most~$1$, thus $1 \ge \sum_t \delta_t = B(\epsilon)$. 
  Hence, $B$ is a semimeasure and the lemma is proven.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Bob's strategy does not depend on~$\varepsilon$. 
  The idea is that Bob plays the above strategy simultaneously for infinitely many~$C$. 
  To guarantee $B(\epsilon) \le 1$, we need to push slightly smaller flows.  Let \[C_i = i(i+1)2^i.\]
  \begin{algorithm}[H]
    \caption{Bob's reply.} 
    \algtext*{EndFor}{}
    \algtext*{EndWhile}{}
    \algtext*{EndIf}{}
    \begin{algorithmic}[1]
      \While{integer $i\ge 1$ and $x_1 \sqsubset \cdots \sqsubset x_{C_i}$ exist with $w(x_j) >2^{-i}B(x_j)$ for all $j = 1, \ldots, C_i$} 
	     \State $\delta\;\;\;\;\;\; \gets \min \{2^i w(x_j) - B(x_j): j = 1, \ldots, C_i\}$
	     \State $B(z) \gets B(z) + \delta$ for all $z \sqsubseteq x_{C_i}$ 
	  \EndWhile
    \end{algorithmic}
  \end{algorithm}
  As before, $B(z) \ge B(z0) + B(z1)$. To see that $B(\epsilon) \le 1$, consider the sets of rounds $R_i$ where flow is pushed for value~$i$. 
  Let $B = \sum B'_i$ where $B'_i$ corresponds to all flows pushed during rounds in $R_i$. 
  For each $B'_i$, we have 
  \[
    \sum_x w(x) \ge \sum_x \Big| w(x) - \frac {B(x)}{2^i} \Big|_+ + \sum_{t \in R_i}  i(i+1)\delta_t 
  \]
  for exactly the same reasons as in lemma~\ref{lem:weightflow_easy}, 
  but now $B$ gets a $\delta_t$ increase in $C_i = i(i+1)2^i$ places (instead of $2^i$), 
  which implies that the sum decreases by $i(i+1)\delta_t$. 
  Thus, $\sum \{\delta_t : t \in R_i\} \le \tfrac 1 {i(i+1)}$. 
  After summing over $i$, we see that $\sum_t \delta_t \le 1$ and hence, $B$ is indeed a semimeasure. 

  It remains to verify the winning condition. 
  Fix $\omega$. First assume that all prefixes of $x$ satisfy $w(x)/B(x) \le 1$.  
  For each $i$, there are at most $C_i-1$ prefixes~$x$ with $2^{-i} < w(x)/B(x) \le 2^{-i+1}$. 
  Thus,
  \[
    \sum_{x \sqsubset \omega}\left( \frac {w(x)} {B(x)} \right)^{1+\varepsilon}  
    \le \sum_{i=1}^\infty (C_i-1) \cdot (\frac 2 {2^{i}})^{1+\varepsilon} 
    < 2^{1+\varepsilon} \sum_{i=1}^\infty i(i+1)2^{-\varepsilon i} 
    \le \frac {4 \cdot 2} {(1-2^{-\varepsilon})^3}. 
  \]
  Unfortunately, it may happen that $w(x)/B(x) > 1$, but there are at most $C_1 - 1 = 3$ such strings. 
  For this we modify the $B$ flow so that the ratio is always bounded by $2$. Let
  \[
    B'(x) = \tfrac 1 2 B(x) + \tfrac 1 2 \sum_{z:x \sqsubseteq z} w(z). 
    \]
    The ratio $w(x)/B'(x) \le 2$. The sum for $B'$ contains an additional factor $2^\gamma$ plus the contribution of at most $3$ larger terms. 
    Hence, Bob wins the game for 
    \[
      s = 2^\gamma (\frac {8} {(1-2^{-\varepsilon})^3} + 3).
    \]
  Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_eps} is proven.
head: environment

label: lem:upper_bound_gamma1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:upper_bound_gamma1}
  Bob has a winning strategy in the weight-flow game for $\gamma = 1$ and some $s = O(\log^2 N \log^4 \log N)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We start by analysing the finite game restricted to $N$-bit strings where $N \ge 2$. 
  The algorithm is the same as for lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_eps}, but using better coefficients $C_i = \lceil \log N\rceil 2^i$. 

  For notational convenience, we ignore the first few terms in the sum of the winning condition, 
  equivalently, we assume $0 = w(\epsilon) = w(0) = w(1) = \ldots$, since finitely many terms do not matter given the big-O notation in~$s$.  
  For this, we need that the ratios $w(x)/B(x)$ are bounded on those finitely many strings, 
  and this is achieved by adding a uniform flow to Bob's flow and rescaling proportionally. 
  Note that this rescaling factor is absorbed in the big-$O$.

  Note that only flows are pushed for values of $i$ with $C_i \le N$, thus $i \le \lceil \log N \rceil$. 
  If all prefixes of $x$ satisfy $w(x)/B(x) \le 1$, then
  \[
    \sum_{x \sqsubset \omega_{\le N}} \frac {w(x)} {B(x)}
    \le \sum_{i=1}^{\lceil \log N\rceil} (C_i-1) \cdot \frac 2 {2^{i}}
    < O(\log^2 N). 
  \]
  There might be $C_1 \le O(\log N)$ prefixes $z$ for which $w(z)/B(z) > 1$, but in a similar way as before, we bound their ratio by~$2$. 

  Now we need a strategy for all lengths~$N$. 
  For this, we run infinitely many strategies of Bob in parallel where each strategy $w_\ell$ is supported 
  on strings whose lengths are in the interval $[M_\ell, M_{\ell + 1}-1]$ where
  \[
    M_\ell = 2^{2^\ell}.
  \]
  Thus, $w_\ell(x) = w(x)$ if $M_\ell \le |x| < M_{\ell + 1}$ and 0 otherwise. 
  Bob's strategy strategy is 
  \[
    B(x) = \sum_\ell \frac {B_\ell(x)} {\ell(\ell + 1)}. 
  \]
  We verify that Bob is winning.
  \begin{align*}
    \sum_{x \sqsubset \omega_{\scaleobj{0.8}{\le}N}} \frac {w(x)} {B(x)}
    & \le \sum_{\ell=1}^{\lceil\log \log N\rceil} \sum_{n = M_\ell}^{M_{\ell+1}-1} \ell(\ell+1) \frac {w_\ell(\omega_{\scaleobj{0.8}{\le}n})} {B_\ell(\omega_{\scaleobj{0.8}{\le}n})} \\
    & \le \sum_{\ell=1}^{\lceil\log \log N\rceil} \ell^2 \cdot O(\log^2 M_\ell). 
  \end{align*}
  Finally, we observe that $\log M_\ell$ increases geometrically, thus
  \[
    < O(\log^2 N \log^2 \log N). 
    \qedhere
  \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply lemmas~\ref{lem:weightflow2flowflow_Bob}, \ref{lem:game2thm_1tree} and~\ref{lem:upper_bound_eps} 
  (respectively lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_gamma1}) to obtain the proof of the first part (respectively second part). 
  Let $p$ be a program that decides the tree $T$. Then, we have that $\operatorname{K}(p) \le |p| + 2\log |p|$. 
  Thus $2^{\operatorname{K}(T)} \le k^2 2^k$. The theorem is proven.
head: environment

label: lem:BobWinsClassificationGame
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:BobWinsClassificationGame}
  Fix $\gamma > 1$. 
  If $T_1, \ldots, T_{2^k}$ are trees obtained in the above way from classifiers, 
  then Bob has a computable winning strategy for some $s \le O(k^{1+\gamma})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T_1, \ldots, T_{2^k}$ be a list of leafless trees that contain all $T_f$ for classifiers $f$ 
  that are computed by programs of length less than~$k$ within time bound~$t$. 
  Such a list can be made uniformly computable in $k$
  by applying the same technique as in the the construction of maximal semimeasures: 
  interpret each string of length less than $k$ as a program that 
  computes such a tree, possibly by fixing the output if a program terminates too slowly or gives invalid output (for example, produces a leaf). 
   
  Theorem~\ref{th:classifiers_upper} follows from lemma~\ref{lem:game2thm} applied to trees $T_1, \ldots, T_{2^k}$ 
  and the strategy from lemma~\ref{lem:BobWinsClassificationGame}.
head: environment

label: def:
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:}
  A  {\em leafless forest} $F$ is a subset of $\{0,1\}^*$ such that for all $x \in F$, either $x0 \in F$ or $x1 \in F$.
head: environment

label: def:
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:}
  A tuple $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ of forests is called a {\em good partition} of the leafless trees $T_1, \ldots, T_K$~if
  \\-- $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ partitions all nodes in $T_1 \cup \ldots \cup T_K$, 
  \\-- forests $F_j$ are leafless,
  \\-- if a node $v$ in a tree $T_i$ has a single child, then $v$ has a single child in the forest $F_j$ containing $v$,
  \\-- the intersection of a branch $\omega$ and a forest $F_i$ is either empty or a path, 
  thus $\{n : \omega_{\scaleobj{0.8}{\le}n} \in F_i\}$ is an interval in $\mathbb N$ (possibly empty or infinite).
head: environment

label: lem:flowflow2weightflow_Bob_manyTrees
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:flowflow2weightflow_Bob_manyTrees}
  Assume forests $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ are a good partition of leafless trees $T_1, \ldots, T_K$. 
  Also, assume that Bob has a winning strategy in the weight-flow game with parameters $\gamma$ and~$s$. 
  Then Bob has a winning strategy in the flow-flow game on the trees $T_1, \ldots, T_K$ with parameters $\gamma$ and $2^\gamma k(1 + k^\gamma s)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will use $k$ copies of the weight-flow, where
  for Alice, a strategy $w_j$ in the weight-flow game is obtained by increasing~$w$ 
  for each flow that leaves forest $F_j$ from a node in~$F_j$. 
  For Bob, a strategy is obtained in the flow-flow game by pushing the flow 1 step forward on nodes with 1 child in its forest. 
  Here are the details. 

                                                        
                                                                                                                            
  Let $A_{\textnormal{ff}}$ be a move by Alice in the flow-flow game. Recall that $F_j$ is leafless.  

  \medskip
  \noindent
  {\em Alice's move $w_j$ in the $j$-th weight-flow game.} 
  Let $w_j(x) = A_{\textnormal{ff}}(xb)$ if $x \in F_j$ and $xb \in \partial F_j$ for some bit~$b$. For all other $x$, let $w_j(x) = 0$. 

  \medskip
  \noindent
  Note that $\sum_x w_j(x) \le 1$, because $\partial F_i$ is prefix-free. 
  
  \medskip
  \noindent
  {\em Bob's move in the flow-flow game.} 
  Let $B_{\textnormal{wf},j}$ be the reply from Bob when he plays a winning strategy against Alice's move~$w_j$. 
  Flow $B_{\textnormal{ff}}$ is obtained by pushing each flow $B_{\textnormal{wf},j}$ for 1 step forward on nodes $p$ that have a unique child $pb$ in the direction of $pb$, 
  and taking the average over these $B_{\textnormal{wf},j}$ and $A_{\textnormal{ff}}$'s flows. 

  Formally, let $B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'(x) = B_{\textnormal{wf},j}(p)$ if $p$ is the parent of $x$ and $p$ has exactly 1 child $x$ in its forest. If $p$ has 2 children, then $B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'(x) = B_{\textnormal{wf},j}(x)$. 
  If $x$ is on a path to at least 1 root of forest $F_j$, then let $B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'(x)$ be the sum of all flows $B_{\textnormal{wf},j}(r)$ over roots~$r$ that are extensions of~$x$. 
  If $x$ is neither on $F_j$ nor on a path to some of its roots, then $B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'(x) = 0$. 
  Finally, for all $x$, we set 
  \[
    B_{\textnormal{ff}}(x) = \tfrac 1 2A_{\textnormal{ff}}(x) + \tfrac 1 {2k} \sum_{j \le k} B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'(x). 
  \]

  \medskip
  \noindent
  For the same reasons as before, $B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'$ is a semimeasure, thus so is~$B_{\textnormal{ff}}$. 
  It remains to verify that Bob wins the game with parameters $\gamma$ and $k2^\gamma (1 + k^\gamma s)$. 

  Fix a tree $T_i$ and an infinite branch $\omega$. We need to bound
  \[
    \sum_{\substack{n: \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \in T_i \\ \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T_i}} 
    \left( \frac {A_{\textnormal{ff}}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n)} {B_{\textnormal{ff}}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \omega_n) + B_{\textnormal{ff}}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar \omega_n)} \right)^\gamma.
        
                                                                                           
                                                                                                                   
  \]
  We rewrite this so that the winning condition of the weight-flow game can be used, which requires to think about forests.  

  All flow that leaves tree $T_i$ also leaves some forest $F_j$, except in those nodes where the tree $T_i$ leaves a forest $F_j$,
  see figure~\ref{fig:winningcondition_forests}.  
  This exceptional flow stays in the forest, and this flow is not accounted for in any game. There is 1 such term per forest. 
  \[
    \sum_{\substack{n: \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \in T_i \\ \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in T_i}} \cdots \quad 
    \le \quad \sum_{j \le k} \textnormal{Missing}_j  + \sum_{\substack{n: \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \in F_j \\ \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in F_j}} \cdots 
  \]
  Since $B_{\textnormal{ff}} \ge \tfrac 1 2 A_{\textnormal{ff}}$, each (missing) term is at most $2^\gamma$. Hence, we need to bound
  \[
    \le 2^\gamma k  + \sum_{j \le k} \sum_{\substack{n: \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \in F_j \\ \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in F_j}} 
    \left( \frac {A_{\textnormal{ff}}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n)} {B_{\textnormal{ff}}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \omega_n) + B_{\textnormal{ff}}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar \omega_n)} \right)^\gamma.
  \]
  Note that if $x$ has 1 child $xb$ in $F_j$, then $B_{\textnormal{wf},j}(x) = B_{\textnormal{ff},j}'(xb)$. 
  By definition of $w_j$, 
  \[
    \le 2^\gamma k  + \sum_{j \le k} \sum_{\substack{n: \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \in F_j \\ \omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n} \bar\omega_n \not\in F_j}} 
    \left( \frac {w_j(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n})} {\tfrac 1 {2k} B_{\textnormal{wf},j}(\omega_{\hspace{-1pt}\scaleobj{0.8}{<}\hspace{-.5pt} n})} \right)^\gamma.
  \]
  Now the lemma finishes by using that Bob is winning the weight-flow games, thus
  \[
    \le 2^\gamma k + k \cdot (2k)^\gamma s. 
    \qedhere
  \]

label: def:
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:}
  Let $T$ be a tree. 
  \\-- A node $z \in T$ is called {\em splitting} if both $z0 \in T$ and $z1 \in T$. 
  \\-- A node $z \in T$ is called {\em predicting} if it has exactly 1 child in~$T$.  
  \\-- Trees $T_1, \ldots, T_K$ are called {\em jointly predicting} if for every $z$, either 
  all trees that contain $z$ are splitting or all are predicting.
head: environment

label: lem:getForests
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: The output $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ of \textsc{ForestConstruction} partitions $T_1 \cup \cdots \cup T_K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Claim.} 
  {At the beginning of the $i$-th iteration of the for loop in \textsc{ForestConstruction}, 
  every remaining node in $U$ lies on less than $2^{k + 1 - i}$ trees.} 

  \medskip
  \noindent
  Proof of the claim.
  Since the root lays on less than $2^k$ trees, this holds for $i = 1$. 

  Now inductively assume the claim for some $i$, thus we assume every node in $F_i$ 
  lays on less than $2^{k+1-i}$ trees. 
  Every node in $F_{i+1}$ was not added to $F_i$, and such a decision can happen only in the else case inside~\textsc{Process}. 
  It happens only for the child that lays on the smaller number of nodes. Thus this number is smaller than $2^{k+1-i}/2 = 2^{k+1-i-1}$. 
  The inductive step and hence the claim are proven. 

  \medskip
  \noindent
  This implies that at the beginning of the $k$-th iteration, every node in $U$ lies on exactly 1 tree and \textsc{Process} copies $U$ into $F_k$. 
  Hence, the forests $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ cover all the trees.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is easy to see that the forests are computable, because the decision to include a node $x$ in some forest only depends on 
  the part of the trees on strings of length at most~$|x|$. 

  It remains to verify that $F_1, \ldots, F_k$ is a good partition of $T_1, \ldots, T_K$. 
  The previous lemma states that it is a partition. 

  At any moment, $U$ is leafless because the copying to $F_j$ always starts from a root in~$U$. 
  Hence, each $F_{j+1}$ is leafless, because the most popular child always exists and the copying never terminates. 

  If a node $v$ contains 1 child in a tree $T_i$, then this node is predicting and has 1 child in the forest containing~$v$. 

  Finally, observe that each infinite branch $\omega$ of a tree $T_i$ intersects $F_j$ in a path. 
  Indeed, each ``less popular child'' finishes the copying of the prefix to the current~$F_j$. 
                                                                               
  Afterwards, no more prefixes are copied from~$\omega$. 

  In conclusion, the forests are a good partition. 
  Lemma~\ref{lem:getForests} and hence theorem~\ref{th:classifiers_upper} are proven.
head: environment

label: lem:lowerbound_strategy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Select $N$ of the form $2^{2^\ell}$. Note that $2^{\operatorname{K}(N)} \le O(\log^2 \log N)$.  
  The theorem now follows from lemmas~\ref{lem:game_lowerbound} and~\ref{lem:weightflow2flowflow_Alice}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This proof follows the main technical result in~\cite{Andreev2016sum}, which is their lemma~4.  
  We note that their strategy is uniformly computable and has the following property. 
  After every move of Alice and before Bob's move, Alice is in a winning position in a certain string $x$. 
  If Bob invalidates this winning position, then Alice will never attempt to recover the winning position in $x$, but instead create a winning position in another string. 
  The proof shows that eventually, some string becomes winning for Alice and remains winning forever. 

  
                                                                                                              
                                                                       

  We only explain the changes, which involves estimating the error when approximating a finite sum by an integral. 

  The construction of the strategy is recursive in the target~$s$: given a strategy for parameter $s$, 
  a new strategy is obtained with parameter $s + 2^{-\lceil 4s\rceil}$ using strings of length at most~$\lceil 5s\rceil$ and playing the recursive strategies at the end of each string, 
  see figure~\ref{fig:concatenate_lowerbound_strategies}. 

  Let the gain be $\varepsilon = 2^{-\lceil 4s\rceil}$ and the number of strings be~$n = 2^{\lceil 5s\rceil}$. 
  For this, we need to find values of $\beta_i$ and $d_i$ such that $\sum \beta_i \ge 1$ where 
  both quantities are obtained from $(*)$ and $(**)$ on page 11 of~\cite{Andreev2016sum}. 
  Here $\beta_i$ is the bound of the game on the $i$-th string.
  The equations are 
  \begin{align*}
    \frac{s(1-\varepsilon)(1-\tfrac i n)} {1-d_i} & = s + \varepsilon \\
    s + \varepsilon - \tfrac {\varepsilon} {d_i} = s \frac {(1-\varepsilon)/n} {\beta_i}. 
  \end{align*}
  Let $t_i = \varepsilon + \tfrac i n (1-\varepsilon)$. 
  We have
  \[
    \beta_i = \frac {(1-\varepsilon)(\varepsilon + st_i)} {n(s + \varepsilon)t_i}. 
  \]
  Note that $\beta_i$ is decreasing in~$i$.  One has 
  \[
    \sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i = \frac  {1-\varepsilon} {n(s+\varepsilon)} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac {\varepsilon + st_i} {t_i}  \ge \frac  {1} {s+\varepsilon} \int_\varepsilon^1 \frac {\varepsilon + su}{u} \mathrm d u - \beta_0 + \beta_n.
  \]
  Solving the integral gives
  \[
    = \frac {\varepsilon \ln \tfrac 1 \varepsilon + (1-\varepsilon)s} {s+\varepsilon} - \beta_0 + \beta_n.
  \]
  One verifies that for $\varepsilon = 2^{-\lceil 4s\rceil}$, $n = 2^{\lceil 5s\rceil}$ and $s \ge 1$, this bound is indeed at least~$1$. 
                                                                               

  It remains to verify that the length of the strings needed for this stratagey is $2^{cs}$ when $s \ge c$. 
  Indeed, to increase $s$ from $i-1$ to $i$ (with $i$ integer), 
  we need to repeat this construction at most $2^{4i}$ times. 
  Thus, to reach a value $s-1$, the total length of the concatenated strings is 
  \[
    \sum_{i = 1}^{s} 5i \cdot 2^{4i} \le O(s 2^{4s}). 
  \]
  Thus there exists a constant $c$ such that this is at most $2^{c(s-1)}$ if $s-1 \ge c$. 
   Lemma~\ref{lem:lowerbound_strategy} is proven.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that in the proof of  lemma~\ref{lem:weightflow2flowflow_Alice}, 
  we can choose a tree in which the predicted bits are precisely those in even position, 
  and the prediction is always zero.
  This tree corresponds to any classifier that maps both strings ``0'' and ``1'' to the bit $0$. 
  This almost works, but there is a small problem, because we need to assume a prefix encoding of the strings in the input stream. 
  But the fix is obvious, the tree should alternate predicting layers with several branching layers according to the prefix encoding.

label: def:evenSemimeasure
title: Definition
body_md:
An {\em online} semimeasure $P_{\textnormal{on}}$ is a function that maps lists of the form $x_1, b_1, x_2, b_2, \ldots, x_n$ or $x_1, b_1, x_2, b_2, \ldots, x_n, b_n$ 
  with $x_i \in \{0,1\}^*$ and $b_i \in \{0,1\}$ to $\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$ that satisfy
     \begin{flalign*} 
       \;\;\bullet\;\; & P_{\textnormal{on}}(\textnormal{empty list})  \le 1, & \\ 
       \;\;\bullet\;\; & P_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, b_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}, b_{n-1})  = P_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, b_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}, b_{n-1}, x_n), & \\ 
       \;\;\bullet\;\; & P_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, b_1, \ldots, x_{n})  \ge \sum_{\!\!b_n \in \{0,1\}\!\!} P_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, b_1, \ldots, x_n, b_n). & 
  \end{flalign*}
head: environment

label: prop:algorithmicOnlineProbability
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:algorithmicOnlineProbability}
  Among the lower semicomputable online       
  semimeasures, there exists a semimeasure ${M}_{\textnormal{on}}$ that is maximal up to a constant factor, 
  thus for each such semimeasure $P_{\textnormal{on}}$ one has $\exists c \forall L[P_{\textnormal{on}}(L) \le c {M}_{\textnormal{on}}(L)]$.
head: environment

label: prop:errorOnlineClassification
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{prop:errorOnlineClassification}
  
  If $f$ is computed by a program of prefix-complexity~$k$, then for each sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots \in \{0,1\}^*$,
  \[
    \sum_{n=1}^\infty 1 - {\widetilde M}_{\textnormal{on}}(f(x_n) \,|\, h_n, x_n) \,\le\, k\ln 2 + O(1).
  \]
head: environment

label: cor:classifiers_difference
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:classifiers_difference}
  There exists a computable classifier $f$ and infinitely many $N$ for which there exist strings $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N \in \{0,1\}^*$ such that 
  \[
    \lim_N \sum_{n=1}^N 1 - M(f(x_n) \,|\,  h_n, x_n) = +\infty 
    \qquad \text{ and } \qquad  
    \sum_{n=1}^N 1 - {\widetilde M}_{\textnormal{on}} (f(x_n) \,|\, h_n, x_n) \le O(1). 
  \]
  where $h_n = [x_1, f(x_1), \ldots, x_{n-1}, f(x_{n-1})]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows~\cite[theorem 3.8.9]{Hutter2024book}. Since $1-a \le \ln \tfrac 1 a$ for all $a > 0$, 
  \[
      \sum_{n=1}^\infty 1 - {\widetilde M}_{\textnormal{on}}(f(x_n) \,|\, h_n, x_n) 
     \le \sum_{n=1}^\infty \ln \frac 1 {{\widetilde M}_{\textnormal{on}}(f(x_n) \,|\, h_n, x_n)}. 
   \]
   Expanding the definition of conditional online complexity, 
   \[
     \le \ln \Big(\frac {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1)} {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, f(x_1))} \cdot \frac {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, f(x_1), x_2)} {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, f(x_1), x_2, f(x_2))}
		  \ldots \cdot \frac  {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(h_n, x_n)} {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(h_n, x_n, f(x_n))}\Big).
    \]
   By definition of online semimeasure, each denominator cancels with the next numerator. 
   Thus this equals 
   \[
     \ln \frac  {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(\textnormal{empty list})} {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(h_\infty)} \le \ln \frac 1 {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(h_\infty)}. 
   \]

   \medskip
   \noindent
   Now it remains to show that $-\log {M}_{\textnormal{on}}(h_\infty) \le \operatorname{K}(q) + O(1)$ where $q$ is a program that computes~$f$ on some (plain) reference machine~$V$. 
   As usual, we do this by constructing an online semimeasure $P_{\textnormal{on}}$ and invoking optimality from proposition~\ref{prop:algorithmicOnlineProbability}. 
   Let $U$ be the optimal prefix machine in the definition of $\operatorname{K}$ and let 
   \[
     P_{\textnormal{on}}(x_1, b_1, \ldots, x_n, b_n) = \sum \{2^{-|p|} : V(U(p), x_i) = b_i \text{ with } i = 1, \ldots, n\}.
   \]
   Since $U$ is prefix-free, one has $P_{\textnormal{on}}(\textnormal{empty list}) \le 1$. 
   For lists ending with $x_n$, let $P_{\textnormal{on}}$ be defined by dropping $x_n$.  
   By construction, $P_{\textnormal{on}}(h_\infty) \ge 2^{-k}$ if $f$ is computed a program of prefix-complexity $k$. 
   By definition of ${M}_{\textnormal{on}}$, one has ${M}_{\textnormal{on}} \ge \Omega(P_{\textnormal{on}})$, thus 
   \[
     \log \tfrac 1 {{M}_{\textnormal{on}}(h_\infty)} \le \log \tfrac 1 {P_{\textnormal{on}}(h_\infty)} + O(1) \le k + O(1).
   \]
   The proposition is proven.
head: environment
